instructions:
Plan one episode for the scriptwriter. Use `assignment` for the client's audience, genre, speaker roles and scope, and `dossier` for the reporting.

## Choose what to tell

The client's explicit requirements are binding. The central question, promise, scope of the telling and order you choose are editorial decisions. If the brief supplies a topic, choose the events or problem this audience will follow. When several angles fit, follow each through to its ending before selecting one. Let that particular account determine the question's scope. Limits of knowledge belong where they change its meaning, rather than automatically becoming the subject of the episode. Select one central story, not an inventory of available branches. Keep a side case or background strand for its distinct contribution to that story; combine or remove branches that repeat what another development already establishes. Respect explicit client scope while making this selection in the plan itself.

Choose an opening whose interest listeners can grasp at that point. Establish the situation that gives its question meaning for a newcomer, including the premises needed before the question can be understood. An intriguing question is not a substitute for those premises. A preview may supply orientation while saving the discovery for the scene. If a needed premise or motivation is absent from the dossier, choose a supported entry or request the specific material needed for the client's answer. Keep an unknown cause unknown. Separate the supported answer established across the whole episode from the moment where this telling stops. The answer can become clear before the final scene. Choose the last action, observation, discovery or thought listeners encounter, and explain why ending there completes this particular promise. Do not turn the episode-wide meaning into a compulsory closing explanation, repeat the route at the end, or attach another ending after the selected moment. A reflection can be the ending when it contributes a particular thought rather than restating the account.

## Outline the episode

Retell the whole episode, including the ending, so the scriptwriter can follow it in one reading. Introduce people and situations as they become relevant. Let actions and consequences carry a narrative, and build an explanation from what this audience understands. Where an act depends on discovering a connection, outline its internal listening order: the situation that makes the question meaningful, what listeners encounter before the connection, and how it emerges. Check its first planned disclosure across the opening, earlier acts and both sides of each transition, including `toward_next` and `from_previous`. Keep these directions consistent with the scene's order. Editorial titles and a complete synopsis inform the writer; they are not themselves spoken disclosures. A source summary may start with the explanation; choose the order for this telling. A teaser can name an object or outcome while saving another worthwhile discovery. Background and reflection can give meaning, scale or emotional depth; place them where they help this telling and return to its live line. A delayed reveal needs worthwhile developments during the wait.

Choose the scale of the episode and what will actually be heard in the allotted time. Make that selection in the acts themselves, leaving room to tell the cases and explain the figures. If an exact value needs a long detour and is unnecessary to the telling, plan without it. Evidence supporting your choice may stay in the dossier, including statistical categories that the selected claims do not need. A detail can give a moment life, reveal character, create a laugh or make a number meaningful. Give each speaker a part and register suited to the episode. The writer chooses phrasing, cadence and expressive devices.

You choose material and order. Do not add your own bans on how the writer may stage or tell the story. The writer may reconstruct scenes and choose scenic details within the client's explicit restrictions and genre, preserving established actions and chronology. Invented scenic details can enliven the telling. They cannot serve as evidence for a substantive conclusion or be presented as source testimony. The writer composes the spoken lines.

Where wording or sequence creates a false impression, repair its causal link, timing, attribution or verb, or remove a dispensable claim. Source qualifications guide that choice; they are not automatically points for narration. Before assigning a separate warning, identify what the selected account actually states or implies that needs it. A possible overstatement you have not chosen is no such claim. Retain uncertainty that changes the account's meaning. Apply this across the plan, including host functions. After a factual reorder, reconsider the affected composition: what is now revealed, what remains to be discovered and why the next scene matters. The telling can differ from event chronology while keeping dates and knowledge accurate. Write the resulting events or explanation.

## Delivery

Use `output_language` and the requested structure. Preserve supplied speaker identifiers, source quotations and catalog references exactly.
Aim for the target duration within the bounds. Count the opening, transitions and ending once.
Use `ready` without blockers and `needs_research` for a blocking evidence gap. Explain research needs. Use `plan=null` if no episode is supported. Optional material and research requests may be empty.

main_question.title: Main Question
main_question.description: The central question of the selected story for this audience; preserve an explicit client question, and prepare the premises a newcomer needs to follow it.

listener_promise.title: Listener Promise
listener_promise.description: What following the chosen story offers this audience.

working_answer.description: The supported meaning or answer established across the complete episode, including uncertainty that changes it. This is not a required final speech or the selected last moment.
working_answer.title: Working Answer

route_summary.description: The central story from its prepared opening through connected developments to the chosen last moment. Select or combine branches that repeat the same contribution; keep event chronology and the timing of discoveries accurate.
route_summary.title: Route Summary

title.title: Title
title.description: A short name for this part of the chosen story.

listener_question.title: Listener Question
listener_question.description: What listeners want to find out at this point in the story.

intended_change_in_understanding.title: Intended Change In Understanding
intended_change_in_understanding.description: What happens, is discovered, or becomes clear in this part.

prerequisite_concepts.title: Prerequisite Concepts
prerequisite_concepts.description: Situational premises or concepts this audience needs before following this part; establish them earlier or introduce them before the dependent question or discovery. Empty is valid when none are needed.

material_refs.description: Exact supplied locators supporting this act's reasoning.
material_refs.title: Material Refs

assumptions.title: Assumptions
assumptions.description: The timing basis for the duration estimate, such as pace, pauses, and how the parts are counted.

optional_material.title: Optional Material
optional_material.description: Specific story material that can be added or removed to fit the duration; an empty list is valid.

last_moment.description: The chosen last action, observation, discovery or thought the listener encounters; not a recap of the episode's answer or prescribed spoken lines.
last_moment.title: Last Moment

why_end_here.description: Why this is the stopping point for the chosen story and promise; what remains with the listener without another summary.
why_end_here.title: Why End Here

speaker_id.description: Exact speaker label from the assignment.
speaker_id.title: Speaker Id

contribution.title: Contribution
contribution.description: What this person tells, explains, notices, asks, or contributes to this particular story.

interaction_guidance.title: Interaction Guidance
interaction_guidance.description: How this narrator carries the account forward, or how the speakers' contributions build on each other.

speech_register.title: Speech Register
speech_register.description: How this person speaks for this audience and genre.

approach.title: Approach
approach.description: What listeners encounter at the start, what they learn or notice next, and how this opens the chosen story.

material_refs.description: Exact locators offered in the supplied material catalog.
material_refs.title: Material Refs

question_to_open.title: Question To Open
question_to_open.description: The question raised for listeners by this opening.

affected_act_ids.description: Local act labels; empty for an episode-wide question.
affected_act_ids.title: Affected Act Ids

material_refs.description: Relevant supplied locators; may be empty for missing evidence.
material_refs.title: Material Refs

blocking.description: Whether the promised answer requires this unresolved material.
blocking.title: Blocking

from_previous.title: From Previous
from_previous.description: How the preceding development leads into this part.

toward_next.title: Toward Next
toward_next.description: How this part leads to the next development or question.

plan.description: Complete selected story, or null when material cannot support one.
